item.title: The Vanishing Rate Cut: How One Week of Data Cut September Fed Odds From Near-Certain to One in Three
item.body:
## A Bet That Looked Like a Sure Thing Just Got Shaky

A few weeks ago, traders in the futures market were treating a September interest rate cut from the Federal Reserve almost like a formality. Now, after a stretch of mixed economic data, the mood has shifted noticeably. According to pricing in interest rate futures, the implied probability of a cut at the Fed's September 15-16 meeting has fallen to roughly 32.6% — down sharply from levels that not long ago suggested the move was all but locked in.

That kind of swing in a matter of days says less about any single headline and more about how finely balanced the Fed's decision has become. Markets that were confidently pricing in easing are now hedging their bets, and the reason comes down to two competing signals pulling policymakers in opposite directions.

## Inflation and Jobs Are Sending Mixed Signals

The first piece of the puzzle is inflation. Recent price data came in mixed rather than clearly cooling, which matters a great deal to a central bank whose primary mandate includes price stability. A softer inflation print would have given the Fed more room to justify cutting rates without appearing to abandon its inflation-fighting credibility. Instead, the data left enough ambiguity that policymakers can plausibly argue for either patience or action.

The second piece is the labor market, which has continued to show more resilience than many expected. A jobs market that isn't visibly cracking reduces the urgency for the Fed to step in with lower borrowing costs. Historically, rate cuts have been easier to justify when unemployment is climbing or job growth is clearly slowing. When hiring holds up, the argument for holding rates steady gets stronger, even if other parts of the economy are showing strain.

Put together, these two data points have scrambled what looked like a straightforward calculus. Instead of a near-certain cut, traders are now pricing in real uncertainty about which way the Federal Open Market Committee will lean.

## Stocks Keep Climbing Anyway

What makes this moment especially interesting is that equity markets haven't flinched. Major indexes have continued pushing toward record territory, propelled in large part by blockbuster earnings tied to artificial intelligence infrastructure spending. Companies like CoreWeave have posted results strong enough to keep investor enthusiasm for the AI buildout intact, even as the interest rate outlook grows murkier.

This divergence is worth watching. Normally, a sharp drop in rate cut expectations might be expected to weigh on stock valuations, since lower rates tend to make future corporate earnings look more attractive by comparison. But when a dominant theme like AI infrastructure investment is driving earnings surprises, it can offset — at least temporarily — the drag from a less accommodative rate outlook. Whether that dynamic can hold if the Fed ultimately disappoints rate-cut hopes in September remains an open question.

## Why the Next Few Weeks Matter

With the Fed's meeting just weeks away, every new data release between now and then carries outsized weight. Another inflation report, an updated jobs number, or even comments from Fed officials could easily swing the odds back in the other direction. That is the nature of a "close call" environment: expectations become highly sensitive to incremental information, and market pricing can whip back and forth as a result.

For everyday observers, the key takeaway isn't necessarily which way the Fed will ultimately go — it's how quickly consensus can unravel when the underlying data stops telling a clean, one-directional story. A few months ago, the narrative was simple: inflation cooling, labor market softening, rate cut coming. Now, with inflation data harder to read and hiring proving sturdier than expected, that narrative has splintered.

## The Bigger Picture

This episode is a useful reminder that market-implied probabilities, like the 32.6% figure now attached to a September cut, are not predictions — they're a snapshot of how traders are positioning given the information available right now. Those numbers can and do move substantially in short windows, especially heading into a major policy decision.

As the September meeting approaches, expect volatility in these probability estimates to continue, along with plenty of debate among economists and market strategists about which piece of data — inflation, employment, or something else entirely — will ultimately tip the scale. For now, what once looked like a near-certainty has become a genuine toss-up, and that uncertainty itself has become one of the more notable stories in markets this month.
